description: We are three Health Science students and two Pure and Applied Science students from Marianopolis. We are all interested in exploring the intersection between biomedical science and software engineering. This interest is why we chose to work on a health monitor for astronauts. We believe our different perspectives from Health Science and Pure and Applied Science are our team’s strength. We hope to build a software tool that monitors astronauts’ major body systems and also to have fun.
summary: During long-duration missions, space hazards expose astronauts to develop health risks such as SANS, sleep inertia, and cardiovascular dysrhythmias. These problems can limit mission progress and cause post-flight health complications. Our team developed monitoring software that tracks five main areas of human health: eye health, cardiovascular health, bone health, blood composition, and sleep cycles. For each area, astronauts can track their condition throughout their flight. We identified reference ranges or thresholds for selected indicators, allowing the software to flag measurements that may indicate a potential health concern. We also provide information on countermeasures to help astronauts prevent further health problems. By helping astronauts recognize changes early and understand when further assessment may be needed, our software supports their health and their ability to complete the mission.
details:
Here is the link to our repository: https://github.com/yuxc567-blip/houston_we_re_alive.git

What does it do?

The Houston, We’re Alive software tracks physiological changes caused by the space environment, which may accumulate and affect astronauts’ health. It monitors indicators across five areas: eye health, bone health, sleep, blood health, and cardiovascular health. By comparing measurements with personal baselines and research-based thresholds, it flags changes that warrant attention and provides guidance to help prevent further health problems.

How does it work?

Control Loop and Prevention Algorithm

The objective of the algorithm is to continuously monitor the astronaut's health conditions and help maintain them within an acceptable healthy range. We assume that the system receives periodic measurements of several health indicators as input, such as bone density and other physiological parameters. These measurements are processed individually through a control loop.

1. Health monitoring and error evaluation

For each health indicator, the algorithm compares the astronaut's current measurement with its predefined healthy reference value to calculate the deviation and relative error. This allows the system to quantify how far the current condition is from the desired state.

The algorithm then evaluates two additional aspects of the error over time:

Accumulated error (integral):Uses numerical integration to measure how much deviation has accumulated over time. This helps identify persistent health deterioration that might not be apparent from a single measurement.

Rate of change (derivative): Measures how quickly the error is changing between consecutive measurements. This helps identify rapidly developing health risks, even when the current error is not yet critical.

By combining the current error, accumulated error, and rate of change, the algorithm evaluates the astronaut's health status and assigns an urgency level. This classification helps distinguish between normal conditions, situations requiring attention, and conditions requiring more immediate intervention.

2. Prevention recommendation

Once the urgency level has been determined, the prevention algorithm generates a corresponding recommendation for the specific health indicator.

The system first examines historical records containing previous error measurements and their associated prevention amounts. Using linear regression, it attempts to establish a mathematical relationship between the error level and the prevention amount previously recommended or administered.

If the regression model demonstrates sufficient correlation, determined by a coefficient of determination (R²) meeting the predefined threshold of 0.85, the algorithm uses the fitted regression line to estimate a prevention amount for the current error level. Predictions are restricted to the range of historical observations and must also respect predefined safety limits.

If the historical data is insufficient, the regression model does not meet the required threshold, or the prediction falls outside the permitted range, the algorithm instead provides a predefined recommendation based on the urgency level.

3. Continuous monitoring and adaptation

The recommendation and its associated data can be recorded in the database for future analysis. As additional measurements and intervention records become available, the historical dataset can be expanded and the regression model recalculated.

This creates a continuously updated decision-support process in which health conditions are monitored over time and prevention recommendations can be refined as more data becomes available.

What benefits does it have? What does it hope to achieve?

We hope to help astronauts recognize concerning changes earlier and take an active role in maintaining their health. With further validation, the software could support more autonomous health assessment during long missions and help crews communicate useful, organized information to flight surgeons.

What tools, coding languages, hard/software was used?

  • Python: measurement processing, interpolation, deviation tracking, and prototype assessment logic.
  • Visual Studio Code: code development and testing.
  • Unity: develop an interactive 3D interface by modeling and rendering a human body to visually represent and monitor astronauts’ health conditions. 
  • GitHub: version control and team collaboration.
  • Python standard library: time calculations, numerical validation, status categories, and automated tests.
  • Research resources: NASA Human Research Program evidence reports and published spaceflight studies.
  • Hardware: a computer running simulated measurements; direct sensor integration is a future development.

      • Translated our mathematical framework into Python code, including integral and derivative calculations for health risk assessment.
      • Implemented linear regression to relate historical health deviations to preventive interventions.
      • Assisted in implementing our predefined class structure and inheritance relationships.
      • Improved code readability and resolved syntax, type, and data conversion errors.
      • Generated the initial 3D framework in Unity, including geometric shapes, materials, and rendering components.
      • Provided a foundation for our team to manually construct and refine the human body model.
